title: Strong extractors for infinite sequences
formal:
Does there exist one deterministic oracle Turing machine \(F\) such that for every pair of infinite binary sequences \(x,y\) with
\[\dim(x)=\dim(y)=\tfrac12\]
and global algorithmic independence as defined below, all computations \(F^{x\oplus y}(i)\), \(i\ge0\), halt with a bit, and the resulting sequence \(z(i)=F^{x\oplus y}(i)\) satisfies
\[\dim^x(z)=\dim^y(z)=1?\]
Here \(\dim^a\) is effective Hausdorff dimension measured with the entire sequence \(a\) available as an oracle. The same machine must work for all promised pairs; it receives no description of their independence constants.

This card takes the explicit dimension-one-half instance in the 2012 question and uses “independent” in the global oracle sense of Calude–Zimand's Definition 2.1. The weaker finitary prefix-independence notion is distinguished below; it is not silently substituted for this premise.
why: The question asks whether two imperfectly random infinite sources can yield information of full asymptotic density that remains incompressible even after either entire source is disclosed. It tests how far the strong-extraction principle from finite information extends to arbitrary individual sequences. The distinction matters because an infinite oracle can expose information beyond any fixed pair of input prefixes.

sentences: The question asks for one computable transformation of two independent infinite binary sequences of effective dimension one half.
Its output must have effective dimension one even when either entire input is available as an oracle.
Independence is the global oracle condition, which is stronger than comparing only finite input prefixes.
The transformation may use unbounded computation but must produce every output bit on every promised input pair.
Known ordinary extraction, finite-string strong extraction and finite-state impossibility results do not settle this stated target.

definitions:
An infinite binary sequence is a function \(a:\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}\), with positions starting at zero. Its length-\(n\) prefix is \(a{\upharpoonright}n=a(0)\cdots a(n-1)\). The join is the interleaving \((x\oplus y)(2i)=x(i)\), \((x\oplus y)(2i+1)=y(i)\).

Fix an optimal plain universal Turing machine and an optimal plain universal oracle Turing machine. For a finite binary string \(u\), let \(C(u)\) be the minimum number of program bits required by the first machine to halt with exactly \(u\) as output. Let \(C^a(u)\) be the corresponding minimum for the oracle machine with access to the entire sequence \(a\): a query at index \(i\) returns \(a(i)\). No time, space or oracle-use bound is imposed. Programs are finite binary strings and are not required to form a prefix-free set. Optimality means simulation of every fixed machine of the same type with an additive constant in program length, uniformly in the oracle for the oracle version. Changing the chosen optimal machines changes the complexities only by constants and does not change the dimensions or independence condition here.

Define
\[\dim(a)=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{C(a{\upharpoonright}n)}n,\qquad
\dim^b(a)=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{C^b(a{\upharpoonright}n)}n,\]
where \(n\) ranges over positive integers. Both dimensions lie in \([0,1]\). The input requirement is equality to one half, not a uniform finite-prefix lower bound with a supplied deficiency. In particular the point at which a lower estimate begins to hold may depend on the sequence and on the estimate's accuracy.

Global algorithmic independence means that there exists a finite constant \(c\ge0\), depending on the pair but not on prefix length, such that for every integer \(n\ge1\),
\[C^y(x{\upharpoonright}n)\ge C(x{\upharpoonright}n)-c\log_2(n+2),\qquad
C^x(y{\upharpoonright}n)\ge C(y{\upharpoonright}n)-c\log_2(n+2).\]
An additive constant can be absorbed into \(c\), so this fixes the logarithmic-loss convention also at small lengths. These are requirements about individual infinite sequences; there is no probability distribution from which inputs must be sampled.

For comparison only, finitary independence requires a constant \(d\ge0\) such that for every \(n,m\ge1\),
\[C((x{\upharpoonright}n)(y{\upharpoonright}m))\ge C(x{\upharpoonright}n)+C(y{\upharpoonright}m)-d\bigl(\log_2(n+2)+\log_2(m+2)\bigr).\]
Juxtaposition here is finite-string concatenation. Global independence implies this condition, but the converse fails; the finitary condition alone is not this card's input promise. The 2007 extraction paper uses “independent” for that weaker condition, whereas the 2010 paper explicitly distinguishes both.

The machine \(F\) has a finite program and input the binary representation of the output position \(i\). It may adaptively query either sequence through the join and use arbitrarily much finite time and space on each halting computation. Each output bit must halt for every promised pair. The machine may diverge on pairs outside the promise, and no computable uniform bound on oracle positions queried is required. There is no additional oracle, random seed or input-dependent advice. A truth-table reduction, which halts on all oracles, would qualify, but that stronger requirement is not imposed.

The output condition means that for each \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an onset \(N\), allowed to depend on \(x,y,\varepsilon\), such that for every \(n\ge N\), both \(C^x(z{\upharpoonright}n)\) and \(C^y(z{\upharpoonright}n)\) are at least \((1-\varepsilon)n\). The two conditionings are separate: the output need not retain dimension one relative to the join, from which it is computable. Ordinary dimension one alone is insufficient, as is a high limsup ratio achieved only along selected prefix lengths. The word “strong” refers here to resistance to either input oracle, not to the distinct limsup notion called effective strong dimension.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed uniform extraction claim. A positive answer must supply one finite oracle-machine program, prove termination for every output bit on every promised pair, and prove both relative liminf-dimension guarantees for its full infinite output. A negative answer must show that every candidate machine has a promised pair on which some bit fails to halt with a bit or one required relative dimension is less than one. Failure of one proposed construction, or an impossibility restricted to finite-state or truth-table transformations, does not by itself refute existence of the general Turing reduction. A finite-string conditional extraction theorem does not meet the infinite-oracle target.

context_blocks.text: The 2012 report explicitly asks for dimension one relative to either source after recalling ordinary two-source dimension amplification. The card preserves its concrete half-dimensional case and makes the oracle meaning of both conditioning and independence explicit.

The 2007 theorem supplies one transformation whose output has every randomness rate below one, hence effective dimension one. Its stated conclusion is ordinary output complexity, without either entire input supplied as side information. It therefore establishes the baseline rather than the strong conclusion.

Calude and Zimand distinguish global and finitary independence, prove that the notions differ, and give a positive independence-production result when the two sources are already fully random. That restricted source class does not cover the half-dimensional inputs required here.
The finite-string result permits high-complexity output even conditional on either finite input. Such finite conditioning does not give free access to all future bits of an infinite input oracle.

The July 2026 finite-state impossibility concerns a different computational model and a different dimension. It is recorded as related later work, not as a resolution of the unrestricted Turing question.
